findings.headline: Households in temporary accommodation increased to 1,428 in Q1, with 724 involving children

findings.headline: FMS Wertmanagement exercised its lender option with a proposed rate increase to 7.77% on a £29m LOBO loan; the council repaid at par on 27 August 2026 and replaced it with PWLB borrowing at 4.69%, avoiding £893,000 in annual costs.
findings.detail: On 20 August 2026, FMS notified the Council of a proposed rate increase from 4.625% to 7.77% on its £29m LOBO loan (Loan Instrument Number 640722AI). The Council exercised its borrower option to repay the loan in full rather than accept the revised rate. The loan and accrued interest were repaid on 27 August 2026. On 2 September 2026, the Council took out a replacement £29m PWLB loan at 4.69% (inclusive of HRA discount) for a two-year term. This refinancing avoided approximately £893,000 in annual interest costs compared with accepting the FMS rate, though it increased annual costs by approximately £19,000 compared to the original FMS rate.
findings.matters: A material LOBO refinancing event with significant cost outcomes demonstrates prudent rate benchmarking and has material implications for 2026/27 debt service budgets.
findings.figures: £29m loan; FMS proposed rate 7.77% (from 4.625%); PWLB replacement rate 4.69%; annual cost avoidance £893,000; annual cost increase versus original FMS rate £19,000
findings.quote: By comparison, the replacement PWLB loan will incur annual interest costs of approximately £1.360 million per annum, resulting in an annual cost avoidance of approximately £893,000.

findings.headline: Non-emergency responsive repairs completion rate falls to 73.8% from 82.4%
findings.detail: The proportion of non-emergency responsive repairs completed within the council's target timescale fell from 82.4% in Q4 to 73.8% in Q1, a deterioration of over 8 percentage points. The council acknowledges that "performance against non-emergency repairs timescales has declined during the quarter". Overdue repairs awaiting completion stand at 1,434 with over 4,000 total repairs in progress.
findings.matters: Falling repair completion rates signal service deterioration, increase disrepair liability, and suggest resource or productivity constraints that may require future investment.
findings.figures: Q3 88%, Q4 82.4%, Q1 73.8%; overdue Q1 1,434; total in progress 4,008
findings.quote: Proportion of non-emergency responsive repairs completed within the landlord's target timescale [LCRA only] (%) 89% 88% 82.4% 73.8%

findings.headline: Overdue fire safety and building safety actions increase to 25% of total from 11%
findings.detail: The percentage of total fire risk and building safety actions that are overdue rose from 11% in Q4 to 25% in Q1. Medium-risk actions increased to 1,362 from 1,326, while total overdue actions stood at 2,024. The council notes these will "continue to receive close management attention".
findings.matters: Growing backlogs of fire and building safety actions represent compliance risk and potential future remedial costs; they may also affect lender confidence in council governance.
findings.figures: % overdue Q3 15%, Q4 11%, Q1 25%; total Q1 2,024; medium-risk Q4 1,326, Q1 1,362
findings.quote: % of total Fire Risk Actions that are overdue 45% 15% 11% 25%

findings.headline: Gas safety compliance falls to 93.2% from 98%, below expected levels
findings.detail: The proportion of homes with all required gas safety checks completed fell from 98% in Q4 to 93.2% in Q1. The council explicitly identifies this as an area requiring close management attention, noting in the summary that there remain "challenges in improving our performance on gas certification".
findings.matters: Gas safety is a statutory compliance requirement; failure to meet thresholds carries legal and reputational risk, and may require emergency remedial spending.
findings.quote: BS01 Proportion of homes for which all required gas safety checks have been carried out (%) 98.7% 98.1% 98% 93.2%

findings.headline: Tenancy evictions due to rent arrears double to 10 in Q1 from 2 in Q4
findings.detail: The number of tenancy evictions due to rent arrears increased sharply to 10 in Q1, up from 2 in the previous quarter, reversing a downward trend. While the absolute numbers are small, this represents a fivefold increase quarter-on-quarter and suggests some tenants are unable to sustain tenancy despite overall improvements in rent collection.
findings.matters: A sudden rise in evictions signals emerging household stress and risks to income stability, even though overall collection performance remains strong.
findings.quote: Number of tenancy evictions due to rent arrears 5 4 2 10

findings.headline: Rent collection sustained above 100% and arrears continue to fall
findings.detail: Rent collected as a percentage of rent due stood at 101.2% in Q1, maintaining the consistent pattern above 100% across all quarters reported. The number of rent accounts with arrears above £10,000 fell to 207 from 303 in Q2, and rent arrears as a percentage of rent roll declined to 6.1% from 8.3%, demonstrating the impact of targeted income recovery.
findings.matters: Strong and improving rent collection is a positive indicator of HRA financial health and suggests that tenant support measures are working despite acute housing pressures.
findings.figures: Q1 rent collected 101.2%; accounts >£10k Q2 303, Q1 207; arrears % Q2 8.3%, Q1 6.1%
findings.quote: Rent collected as a % of rent due for all council tenants 100.7% 100.4% 101.1% 101.2%

findings.headline: Capital works expenditure collapses to £4.284m in Q1 from £109.7m in Q4
findings.detail: Total capital works expenditure on housing fell from £109,711,000 in Q4 to £4.284m in Q1, a 96% reduction. The paper provides no explanation for this dramatic change, whether due to project completion, programme delays, or reprioritisation of the capital budget.
findings.matters: A substantial drop in capital investment raises questions about whether housing improvement plans are on track, whether major schemes have stalled, or whether priorities have shifted; finance directors and lenders would need to understand the cause.
findings.quote: Total capital works expenditure on housing £41,000,000 £67,477,000 £109,711,000 £4.284m

findings.headline: Households in temporary accommodation continue to grow, reaching 1,428 despite lower new placements
findings.detail: The stock of households in temporary accommodation has grown from 1,188 in Q2 to 1,428 in Q1, an increase of 240 households. Households with children in temp accommodation also increased to 724. Although new placements have reduced to 121 in Q1, the paper notes that demand continues to outstrip the availability of permanent housing, indicating the exit rate is slower than desired.
findings.matters: Growing temporary accommodation is a major budget pressure on councils; it signals housing supply constraints and indicates residents are not moving into permanent homes quickly enough, with associated costs and service pressures.
findings.figures: Stock Q2 1,188, Q3 1,372, Q4 1,393, Q1 1,428; with children Q1 724; new placements Q1 121
findings.quote: The number of households living in temporary accommodation continuing to increase

findings.headline: Leaseholder service charge arrears spike to £11.5m from £1.6m in the previous quarter
findings.detail: Day-to-day service charge arrears owed by leaseholders jumped from £1,646,724 in Q4 to £11,496,153 in Q1, a sevenfold increase, with major works arrears also around £10.9m, giving combined arrears exceeding £22m. The paper does not explain the cause of this sudden spike.
findings.matters: This represents a material deterioration in collection performance on leaseholder service charges and could affect the HRA's financial sustainability and cash flow.
findings.quote: Total service charge arrears (£) owed by leaseholders (day to day) £5,273,657 £3,000,965 £1,646,724 £11,496,153

findings.headline: Government funding for affordable housing remains uncertain post-2025 Spending Review
findings.detail: Following the 2025 Spending Review, Camden is awaiting government detail on support for affordable housing delivery. Officers will review options including low-cost borrowing, but the level of funding available is not yet confirmed. This creates uncertainty for the existing Camden Living programme, which has already committed £6.4m to acquire 34 affordable homes with a further 10 expected.
findings.matters: Affordable housing is a stated priority but future delivery depends on government funding that is currently unconfirmed. If support is lower than expected, the council may need additional borrowing or will need to reduce housing targets.
findings.figures: £6.4m already lent to Camden Living Housing Association for 34 homes, further 10 expected
findings.quote: Following the Spending Review 2025, the Council is awaiting further detail on Government support for affordable housing delivery. Officers will continue to review funding opportunities, including the potential use of low-cost borrowing

findings.headline: Borrowing requirement expected to materialise within 12-24 months as reserves deplete
findings.detail: The council's long-term financial modelling indicates that gradual depletion of earmarked reserves will trigger an external borrowing requirement within the next 12-24 months. This marks the timeline when the under-borrowing liability will convert into actual debt issuance and when the council will need to access debt markets.
findings.matters: Lenders should monitor for when Camden enters debt markets for this funding. The scale and timing of this borrowing will depend on how quickly reserves deplete and on market interest rates at that time.
findings.figures: Borrowing requirement expected within 12-24 months, projected CFR growth
findings.quote: Current long-term financial modelling indicates a gradual and planned usage of earmarked reserves which will reduce cash balances and is expected to create a borrowing requirement within the next 12 to 24 months.

findings.headline: Structural funding gap eroding reserves: rising demand and costs outpacing grant income
findings.detail: Camden is drawing down reserves to bridge a structural gap between rising service demand and stagnant grant funding. The council explicitly reports that 'demand for services has continued to increase, while expenditure has risen and funding from grants and other income sources has not kept pace.' A significant proportion of investments were utilised during 2025/26 to support cash flow and meet service delivery requirements, reducing total investments held. This is not a one-time issue but an ongoing structural imbalance.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund ongoing operational gaps is unsustainable and constrains future financial flexibility. Lenders need to understand whether this gap is temporary or a permanent structural problem driven by government funding cuts or rising service costs.
findings.figures: Investment portfolio £197m at 31 March 2026 (reduced from prior year), proportion of investments drawn down to support cash flow
findings.quote: Demand for services has continued to increase, while expenditure has risen and funding from grants and other income sources has not kept pace.

findings.headline: Council deferred £518m borrowing requirement using internal reserves, saving £10.4m in 2025/26 but crystallising a future liability
findings.detail: Camden avoided new external borrowing in 2025/26, using internal resources instead of taking debt at 6.28% rates. The Capital Financing Requirement rose to £812m (from £762m) while external borrowing remained flat at £294m, widening the under-borrowing gap from £468m to £518m. The council saved approximately £10.4 million in carry costs this year but has explicitly acknowledged that this under-borrowing 'represents a deferred liability' that will require external borrowing within 12-24 months as reserves deplete.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know that while the council has avoided near-term debt issuance, it has accumulated a £518m borrowing requirement that will crystallise into actual external debt within 12-24 months. The timing and cost of this borrowing depends on future market conditions and the council's cash position.
findings.figures: CFR £812m (up from £762m), external borrowing £294m (unchanged), under-borrowing £518m (up from £468m), saved £10.4m, PWLB 50-year rate 6.28% in March 2026
findings.quote: No new external borrowing was taken in 2025/26. The internal borrowing policy remains sound and cost-effective, delivering annual savings of approximately £10.4 million.

findings.headline: Lease accounting and IFRS16 implementation remains a significant audit risk, having been unresolved in 2024/25
findings.detail: Accounting for leases was specifically flagged as outstanding audit work in 2024/25 and is now identified as one of five areas providing significant risk of material misstatement for 2025/26 audit focus.
findings.matters: Lease accounting complexity and IFRS16 implementation have proved problematic for the council and represent a material area the auditor cannot yet fully assure.
findings.figures: Performance materiality threshold £21m
findings.quote: Accounting for leases and implementation of IFRS16

findings.headline: Rebuilding assurance will extend through multiple audit cycles, with target return to unmodified opinion not until 2027/28
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that rebuilding assurance takes place over several subsequent audits as the auditor progressively obtains assurance on closing balances, in-year movements, opening balances and prior year comparators. The CIPFA example provided shows this is a multi-year process.
findings.matters: The council faces a prolonged period of non-standard audit opinions, meaning financial reporting confidence will remain impaired for the next two financial years.
findings.figures: Backstop deadline for 2025/26 accounts: 31 January 2027
findings.quote: Following a disclaimer of opinion, it is acknowledged that a process of rebuilding assurance will need to take place over a number of subsequent audits, as assurance is obtained on closing balances, in year movement, opening balances and prior year comparators.

findings.headline: Camden received disclaimed audit opinions for 2024/25 due to incomplete assurance on opening balances and outstanding lease accounting work
findings.detail: This follows disclaimed opinions in 2022/23 and 2023/24. The 2024/25 disclaimer specifically cited incomplete assurance on opening balances, prior year comparators, and outstanding audit work on lease arrangements. The council is not alone—statistics show more authorities received disclaimed opinions than unmodified ones for 2024/25 (188 vs 182).
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions indicate the auditor could not complete necessary checks to verify financial accuracy, suggesting persistent gaps in the council's financial reporting environment that affect confidence in its accounts.
findings.figures: 2024/25: 188 disclaimed (backstop) by backstop date vs 182 unmodified; as at March 2026
findings.quote: For 2024/25 the Council returned to statutory reporting deadlines for publishing draft accounts and a full audit was planned and largely completed by the backstop. The Council received a disclaimed audit opinion due primarily to incomplete assurance on opening balances and prior year comparators, but also outstanding audit work on lease arrangements.

findings.headline: Capital receipts slippage could trigger unplanned additional borrowing if major funding sources are delayed
findings.detail: The council's capital programme relies heavily on capital receipts, which comprise over 40% of its total £1,421.96m funding (HRA capital receipts £441.16m, RTB retained receipts £46.03m, General Fund capital receipts £93.73m). The document explicitly states that slippage of these receipts would necessitate additional borrowing until they are received, while these receipts also repay existing borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of risks that could drive unplanned increases in borrowing beyond the £290.97m of planned prudential borrowing.
findings.figures: Capital receipts total £580.92m (40.8% of £1,421.96m); Prudential borrowing HRA £176.17m, GF £114.80m; Total planned borrowing £290.97m
findings.quote: Any slippage of capital receipts and their high use over the coming years (both to fund the Capital Programme and to repay existing borrowing) would mean the need for additional borrowing until the receipts are received.

findings.headline: Net reserve drawdown of £11.15m represents material consumption of financial buffers
findings.detail: Total net drawdown from reserves is £11.15m to cover overspends across multiple services. This is not capital investment or a one-off adjustment; it is ongoing revenue overspends being covered by running down reserves.
findings.matters: Persistent reserve drawdowns to cover current spending deplete the council's financial resilience and ability to absorb future shocks.
findings.figures: £11.15m net drawdown
findings.quote: A net drawdown from our reserves totalling £11.15m is recommended for 2025/26.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account also overspending, with £2.87m reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The HRA is overspending and drawing £2.87m from its own reserves. This shows budget pressure across both General Fund and Housing accounts.
findings.matters: HRA overspends indicate housing cost pressures and use of housing reserves for current spending rather than investment or maintenance.
findings.quote: £2.87m would be drawn down from Housing Revenue Account (HRA) reserves to meet its overspend

findings.headline: £6.31m High Needs Block overspend with £12.27m total schools reserve drawdown
findings.detail: Schools are drawing £8.07m for additional expenditure plus £4.20m from the High Needs reserve, largely because the High Needs Block (special educational needs) is overspent by £6.31m. This is material and indicates SEND demand continuing to exceed funding.
findings.matters: High Needs overspends are a national issue and signal future budget stress; councils cannot easily control demand for SEND provision.
findings.figures: £6.31m overspend; £8.07m drawdown plus £4.20m
findings.quote: largely driven by the need to fund the £6.31m overspend against the High Needs Block

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation and Social Care named as ongoing pressures requiring £5m reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies Temporary Accommodation and Social Care as driving pressures on the General Fund and is allocating £5m from reserves to manage them. These are demand-led services with no natural cost controls.
findings.matters: Demand-led service pressures are structural and unlikely to resolve without policy intervention, indicating future budget difficulty.
findings.quote: £5m drawdown to help manage the General Fund overspend driven by on-going Temporary Accommodation and Social Care pressures

findings.headline: General Fund overspend of £14.03m being covered by reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council cannot balance its General Fund from current income and is drawing £14.03m from reserves to cover the overspend. This is the largest single drawdown and represents the council consuming its buffer for day-to-day spending.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council is running operational deficits and cannot sustain them without depleting reserves, a sign of structural budget imbalance.
findings.quote: £14.03m of this drawdown would meet the overspend on the General Fund (GF)

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Revenue Estimates and Council Tax Setting
findings.headline: Director of Finance confirms budget is sound conditional on recommendations approved, but flags medium-term outlook as challenging with ongoing sector fragility elsewhere
findings.detail: The Section 25 statement (Paragraph 7.10-7.11) notes that while Camden is not in the position of councils receiving Exceptional Financial Support, it nonetheless faces significant financial pressures. The CFO acknowledges that 'the Council has a strong history of living within its budget, though the pressures of the past two years... have been exceptional' and references 'sector fragility, evidenced by recent Section 114 notices elsewhere.'
findings.matters: A CFO's Section 25 statement noting exceptional pressures and comparing positively to others receiving exceptional support is cautious wording. It signals the council is under material stress but currently managing.
findings.figures: Recent Section 114 notices elsewhere in sector; London-wide funding gap £1bn this year, over £4bn by 2028/29
findings.quote: While the Council is not in this position, it nonetheless faces significant financial pressures both this year and across the medium term. London Councils report a London‑wide funding gap of £1bn this year, rising to over £4bn by 2028/29, driven by prolonged inflation, high interest rates, rising demand, and more than a decade of constrained government funding.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Revenue Estimates and Council Tax Setting
findings.headline: HRA drawing £5m from reserves to balance 2026/27 budget described as temporary solution, with £201m cumulative rental income loss since 2016
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is using a planned £5m drawdown from reserves to balance 2026/27, described as 'a temporary solution' requiring a new savings programme from 2027/28. The HRA has lost £201m of rental income since 2016 due to rent restrictions, with rental income £33m lower in 2025/26 than it would be under CPI+1% policy.
findings.matters: The HRA is ring-fenced but council-dependent for capital investment. Structural imbalance in rental income vs costs, combined with reserve drawdown, signals deteriorating housing asset position and reduced capacity for investment.
findings.figures: £5m HRA reserve drawdown 2026/27; £201m cumulative rental income loss since 2016; £33m annual shortfall vs CPI+1%
findings.quote: The funding strategy is to raise all available income from rents and drawdown £5m as a planned drawdown from the HRA reserve. This is a temporary solution to balance budgets and ensure that there is sufficient time to work on a new savings programme from 2027/28. The HRA has lost £201m of rental income since 2016 and rental income is £33m lower in 2025/26 compared with what it would have received if the policy had been kept consistent at CPI + 1%.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Revenue Estimates and Council Tax Setting
findings.headline: Council tax set at 4.99% increase (maximum threshold before referendum required) due to structural cost pressures and reduced government funding
findings.detail: The 4.99% increase—comprising 2.99% core and 2% Adult Social Care Precept—is at the maximum threshold. Any higher would trigger a referendum. The report states this is driven by 'sustained cost pressures, rising demand for statutory services and the cumulative impact of long term reductions in government funding.'
findings.matters: When a council is already at the maximum tax increase threshold and still faces structural deficits, there is limited room for manoeuvre. This indicates constrained financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 4.99% council tax increase (maximum threshold); 2.99% core + 2% Adult Social Care Precept; Band D charge £1,696.61 (was £1,615.98)
findings.quote: the council tax increase of 4.99% recommended in this report, including the 2% Adult Social Care Precept, reflects the immediate need to respond to sustained cost pressures, rising demand for statutory services and the cumulative impact of long term reductions in government funding. Without action now, these pressures would increasingly undermine the Council's ability to meet its statutory duties

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Revenue Estimates and Council Tax Setting
findings.headline: General Fund earmarked reserves declining from £103.6m to £79.0m (£24.6m drawdown) over 2025/26-2026/27 to fund overspends
findings.detail: The Council is using reserves to fund recurring overspends. Earmarked reserves are forecast to drop from £103.6m at end of 2025/26 to £79.0m at end of 2026/27, a reduction of £24.6m. The Director of Finance explicitly notes this is unsustainable: 'using reserves to fund day to day expenditure is unsustainable over the medium term.'
findings.matters: Depleting reserves to balance revenue budget is a warning sign. Once reserves are exhausted, the council has no cushion against demand shocks or economic change. This trajectory is explicitly flagged as unsustainable by the finance officer.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves £103.6m forecast 31/03/26; £79.0m forecast 31/03/27; £24.6m drawdown; £52.5m drawdown of Business Rates relief reserve
findings.quote: With the ongoing financial pressures still being felt by the Council, it has been increasing difficult to transfer unspent income into our reserves. When money is drawn down from reserves and not replenished in equal or greater proportion, reserves start to deplete, increasing the risk to the Council's financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Revenue Estimates and Council Tax Setting
findings.headline: MTFS savings programme only 80% delivered; £6m savings still outstanding with next MTFS expected to be most challenging in a decade
findings.detail: Of the £27.8m savings in the current MTFS (2023/24-2025/26), only 80% has been delivered, leaving approximately £6m outstanding. The Director of Finance states the next MTFS (from April 2027) is expected to be one of the most challenging the Council has faced in the past decade, with work already underway to identify a refreshed medium-term forecast.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver planned savings erodes confidence in financial planning. Combined with permanent structural pressures, the outlook for the next MTFS is concerning.
findings.figures: £27.8m MTFS savings programme; 80% delivered; £6m outstanding
findings.quote: While the Council has delivered over 80% of the savings set out in the current MTFS, approximately £6m remains to be delivered. It is essential that this period is used to finalise the remaining savings to avoid carrying unresolved pressures into future years. The next MTFS is expected to be one of the most challenging the Council has faced in the past decade.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Revenue Estimates and Council Tax Setting
findings.headline: Adult Social Care facing £13m-£15m unfunded annual pressure over medium term plus £5.9m immediate inflationary uplift required
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes £5.9m for market inflationary uplifts to prevent provider failure. Beyond this, over the medium term the Council expects to have to provide a further £13m-£15m above inflation driven by demographic growth and increasing complexity of need. These are structural, demand-driven pressures.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is a statutory duty and demographic pressures (ageing population, increased complexity) are unlikely to reverse. Unfunded medium-term gap indicates unsustainable budget trajectory.
findings.figures: £5.9m 2026/27 market uplift provision; £13m-£15m annual medium-term unfunded gap
findings.quote: the long term nature of the pressures facing ASC means that over the medium term, the Council expects to have to provide a further £13m-£15m above inflation.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Revenue Estimates and Council Tax Setting
findings.headline: Children's Social Care placement costs reaching £5,795-£21,000 per week with £3m-£5m unfunded annual pressure expected over medium term
findings.detail: Average weekly residential placement costs have reached £5,795 by end November 2025, with joint-funded placements ranging £12k-£21k per week. The Council expects to need an additional £3m-£5m above inflation annually over the medium term to manage these pressures. The sector nationally saw spending increase 68% since 2009/10, rising faster than inflation.
findings.matters: Placement costs for children in care are volatile, driven by market availability rather than council control, and represent a statutory duty that cannot be deferred. Unfunded medium-term pressure is a structural deficit.
findings.figures: £5,795 average weekly cost; £12k-£21k range for complex placements; £3m-£5m annual unfunded gap forecast; 68% spending increase nationally since 2009/10
findings.quote: The average weekly residential placement cost reaching £5,795 by the end of November 2025. Some joint funded placements range from £12k-£21k per week. There remains a clear risk that these cost pressures will continue into 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Revenue Estimates and Council Tax Setting
findings.headline: General Fund forecasting £19.6m overspend in 2025/26 despite £12m TA contingency and £9m children's placement contingency already provided
findings.detail: At Quarter 3 2025/26, the Council is forecasting a General Fund overspend of £19.6m even after providing contingencies totalling £21m for the two main pressure areas. The forecast has only improved since Q1 through recruitment controls and management interventions, not through structural solutions. Historic overspends: £22.8m in 2024/25.
findings.matters: Two consecutive years of material overspends (£22.8m then forecast £19.6m) indicate either demand forecasting failure or structural service deficits. Lenders need to understand whether this is exceptional or structural.
findings.figures: Q3 2025/26 forecast overspend £19.6m; 2024/25 actual overspend £22.8m; £21m contingency provision already exceeded
findings.quote: the Council is forecasting further overspends in 2025/26 due to increases in demand for these statutory services.

findings.headline: Under-borrowed by £541.8m with refinancing risk if interest rates rise unexpectedly
findings.detail: The Council has a Capital Financing Requirement of £838.5m but only £294.3m in actual borrowing, maintaining an under-borrowed position of £541.8m. The strategy assumes interest rates will continue falling. However, the document acknowledges that if rates rise sharply instead, the Council will be forced to source new debt at higher costs when it must eventually refinance this gap.
findings.matters: A material interest rate rise would force the Council to borrow a large sum at unfavourable rates, significantly increasing debt service costs and revenue pressure
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement £838.5m; actual borrowing £294.3m; under-borrowed £541.8m; internal borrowing saved £12.9m this year
findings.quote: Eventually the Council will need to arrange new external borrowing to replace the temporary use of internal resources and there is a risk that it will need to source new debt at a time when interest rates are high.

findings.headline: Forecast cash balance dips will require short-term borrowing to maintain liquidity
findings.detail: The Council forecasts that cash balances may fall negative at certain points during 2026-27, requiring the use of short-term external borrowing. This reflects dependency on capital expenditure timing and the receipt of anticipated funding. The Council's ability to maintain its internal borrowing strategy is explicitly described as 'sensitive' to these cash movements.
findings.matters: The Council will need access to short-term credit markets during the year, and timing failures in funding receipts or capital spend could create immediate borrowing needs
findings.figures: Current cash balances £222.3m; capital expenditure forecast 2025-26: £278.788m; capital financing requirement £838.5m
findings.quote: Forecasts indicate that cash balances may fall into negative territory at certain points during the period of the Strategy, and therefore the continuation of internal borrowing will be actively managed through detailed cashflow forecasting and, where necessary, the use of short-term borrowing to maintain liquidity.

findings.headline: Investment income falling by 130 basis points, reducing non-tax revenue
findings.detail: The average return on the Council's £252.3m investment portfolio has declined from 4.97% last year to a current 4.09%, with a further drop to 3.67% forecast for 2026-27. This sustained fall in returns reduces the financial income supporting the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Lower investment returns directly reduce income available to fund services without equivalent savings or tax increases
findings.figures: 2024-25 average return: 4.97%; current average: 4.09%; 2026-27 target: 3.67%; total investments £252.3m (Camden £54.7m own funds)
findings.quote: The average return on our investments is 4.09% (2024-25 4.97%). The target return for 2026-27 is 3.67%, reflecting what is forecast to be a declining interest environment during the period.

findings.headline: £124m LOBO loans face rising likelihood of rate reset at higher levels
findings.detail: The Council holds £124m in Lenders Option Borrowers Option loans at 4.63% average rate. These loans allow the lender to reset the interest rate every six months. The document explicitly states there is now 'greater likelihood' that lenders will exercise this option, which means rates could be forced upward if market rates have risen, immediately increasing the Council's debt service costs.
findings.matters: LOBO rate resets expose the Council to unexpected cost increases that cannot be avoided once triggered by the lender
findings.figures: £124m in LOBO loans; average rate 4.63%; total debt portfolio £294.3m; weighted average cost 4.93%
findings.quote: Given the broader movement in market interest rates, there is now a greater likelihood that LOBO lenders may choose to exercise their option to renegotiate rates during contractual call dates.

findings.headline: Council implemented hiring freeze in March 2025 due to challenging financial position
findings.detail: In March 2025, the Council introduced controls on all recruitment (new and existing posts) in response to its challenging financial position. All hiring managers must obtain approval from the Executive Director Supporting Communities and the s151 officer before recruiting, with financial position of the service considered in each decision.
findings.matters: A hiring freeze is an emergency financial control measure indicating the council's cash position became constrained during 2024-25. When the s151 officer personally approves every hire, it signals urgent cash preservation measures—a clear sign of financial stress.
findings.figures: Universal freeze applies to all recruitment approvals from March 2025 onwards
findings.quote: In March 2025, in response to its challenging financial position, the Council introduced controls on recruitment for all posts. All hiring managers must obtain the approval of the Executive Director Supporting Communities and the Executive Director Corporate Services (s151 officer) before recruiting.

findings.headline: Council identified structural damage and water damage to operational properties requiring specialist remediation
findings.detail: During 2024-25, the Council identified impairments to some operational properties due to structural issues and water damage. Specialists are being engaged to assess defects, support repair and claims processes, with work planned for the coming year. This indicates a deferred maintenance backlog becoming material.
findings.matters: Building defects require capital spending to remedy and affect asset values. Identification of structural and water damage suggests the council's asset maintenance backlog is material enough to impact financial position and require unplanned capital expenditure.
findings.figures: Not specified; relates to 'some' operational properties with defects to be assessed
findings.quote: The Council identified impairments attributable to some of its operational properties in 2024/25 due to structural issues and water damage. Specialists are being engaged to assess defects, support the repair and claims process, and work is planned for the coming year.

findings.headline: Internal Audit opinion is 'Moderate assurance' with control weaknesses requiring follow-up
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit provided a 'Moderate assurance' opinion for 2024-25, indicating the Council's internal control, risk management and governance systems are adequate but with improvement required. Specific weaknesses included limited assurance on contract management in building repairs and no assurance on design and operation of key controls in concessionary travel.
findings.matters: Moderate assurance means documented weaknesses exist in the control environment. Individual audit reviews produced high-risk rated recommendations in isolated systems. While the HIA notes these are not significant in aggregate, 'Moderate' rating signals the council's financial and operational controls need work.
findings.figures: No specific figures; weaknesses identified in building repairs contract management and concessionary travel service controls
findings.quote: For the year ended 31st March 2025, the HIA has provided a 'Moderate assurance' opinion; the Council's systems of internal control, risk management and governance are adequate, with some improvement required.

findings.headline: External auditor issued disclaimed opinions on 2022-23 and 2023-24 Council accounts due to time constraints
findings.detail: Due to insufficient time before statutory backstop dates, external auditor Forvis Mazars issued disclaimed opinions on Council accounts for 2022/23 and 2023/24. The 2023/24 Pension Fund audit completed but received a qualified opinion because the 2022/23 disclaimer meant auditors could not gain sufficient assurance on prior year comparator data.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions mean the auditor was unable to form any opinion on the accounts. While FRC and MHCLG acknowledge these reflect statutory constraints, lenders require audited accounts for due diligence. Unqualified audit opinions are essential for borrowing confidence.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions issued for Council 2022/23 and 2023/24; Pension Fund 2023/24 qualified opinion
findings.quote: Due to insufficient time to conduct a full audit of the 2022/23 and 2023/24 Council accounts prior to the backstop dates. As such, the external auditor Forvis Mazars has issued a disclaimed opinion on the Council accounts for 2022/23 and 2023/24.

findings.headline: £5.6m increase in bad debt provision for Temporary Accommodation rent arrears due to rising homelessness
findings.detail: The Council identified recovery of temporary accommodation debtors as a significant governance issue. Rising homelessness has increased rent receivable but also bad debt risk, triggering a £5.6m increase in bad debt provision. A TA Income and Rent Arrears Steering Group was established to address collection, with bad debt provision monitored throughout the year.
findings.matters: A £5.6m bad debt provision increase signals residents in temporary accommodation have arrears the council expects will not be recovered. This represents both a lost revenue stream and indicates affordability challenges for the council's most vulnerable residents.
findings.figures: £5.6m increase in bad debt provision for Temporary Accommodation rent arrears
findings.quote: Rising cases of homelessness have resulted in an increase in rent receivable, which has resulted in a £5.6m increase in bad debt provision for Temporary Accommodation rent arrears.

findings.headline: Significant revenue overspends emerged during 2024-25 requiring urgent oversight panel scrutiny
findings.detail: The Council's Executive Director Corporate Services established Oversight Panels in response to emergence of significant revenue overspends during 2024-25 to review overspends and shape mitigations at directorate level. The s151 officer also held individual meetings with each of the three Executive Director colleagues to review Quarter 3 forecast position.
findings.matters: Unplanned mid-year overspends indicate budget management challenges and reduce retained resources. Combined with known structural deficits, in-year overspends signal potential liquidity constraints.
findings.figures: Not specified in the document
findings.quote: Following the emergence of significant revenue overspends during 2024/25, the Executive Director Corporate Services (the Council's Section 151 Officer) instituted a number of Oversight Panels to review overspends and shape mitigations at a directorate level.

findings.headline: Council holds £75m (50% of investment portfolio) on behalf of North London Waste Authority's major infrastructure project, with further NLWA borrowing expected.
findings.detail: The council co-invests £75m of its £151m total investment portfolio on behalf of NLWA, deployed as working capital and reserves for the Energy Recovery Facility. NLWA has borrowed £870m to date (£280m + £250m + £200m + £140m) with further borrowing anticipated in late 2025.
findings.matters: A significant portion of the council's liquid investments are committed to a partner entity's major infrastructure project outside its direct control. This reduces available liquidity and creates exposure to NLWA's project execution risks, cost overruns, and completion delays.
findings.figures: £75 million invested on behalf of NLWA of £151 million total portfolio (50%); NLWA borrowing to date totals £870 million.
findings.quote: As of 30 September 2025 the council held total investment balances of £151 million, of which £75 million was invested on behalf of the NLWA.

findings.headline: Treasury strategy awaiting Spending Review 2025 outcome on affordable housing support before committing to additional borrowing.
findings.detail: The council is awaiting details from the central government Spending Review 2025 on support for affordable housing. Officers are consulting advisors and may recommend updates to the Treasury Management Strategy based on the outcome, potentially including low-interest Green Finance Fund for carbon-positive projects.
findings.matters: Pending central government policy decisions create material uncertainty about future borrowing levels and the structure of funding. This delays strategic clarity on medium-term capital funding and borrowing intentions.
findings.figures: No figures disclosed; timing dependent on government announcement.
findings.quote: The Council is awaiting further details on the support for building affordable housing announced in the Spending Review 2025. Officers, in consultation with professional advisors and wider stakeholders, will consider additional funding, including the use of low interest finance where beneficial, and may recommend updates to its Treasury Management Strategy.

findings.headline: LOBO loan portfolio of £124m faces material rate renegotiation risk as lenders likely to exercise options.
findings.detail: The council holds £124m in LOBO loans at an average rate of 4.43%. The paper notes that given current market conditions, there is now a greater likelihood LOBO lenders will exercise their option to renegotiate rates at contractual call dates. While the council can repay at par, rate increases would raise borrowing costs materially.
findings.matters: Unexpected rate increases on £124m of borrowing could materially impact the revenue budget. This is an identified vulnerability in the current debt portfolio.
findings.figures: £124 million LOBO loans; average interest rate 4.43%; at 6.18% (prevailing rate mentioned for new borrowing) this could add approximately £93k per percentage point of increase.
findings.quote: Given the broader movement in market interest rates, there is now a greater likelihood that LOBO lenders may choose to exercise their option to renegotiate rates during contractual call dates.

findings.headline: Under-borrowing position increased to £560m—the council is deliberately drawing down reserves to avoid expensive external borrowing.
findings.detail: External debt remained flat at £294m while CFR rose to £854m, increasing the under-borrowing gap from £468m to £560m. The council avoided locking in borrowing at 6.18% for 50-year loans (which would cost approximately £9.4 million annually), but is funding the capital requirement from reserves instead.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion reduces financial resilience and limits flexibility to respond to adverse conditions. If capital needs accelerate further or market conditions worsen, the council may face forced expensive borrowing or reserve shortfalls.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing increased from £468 million to £560 million; avoided borrowing would have cost "approximately £9.4 million".
findings.quote: The difference between the CFR and the level of actual external debt represents the Council's under-borrowing position, which increased from £468 million to £560 million in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased £92m to £854m due to accelerated HRA project delivery and IFRS16 lease accounting.
findings.detail: The CFR rose from £762m at year-end to £854m at mid-year, driven by higher-than-planned delivery on major housing projects (Godwin, Crowndale, Abbey Phase 3, Camden and Chester Road hostels) and the introduction of IFRS16 accounting for leases. This represents a material step change in the council's underlying borrowing need.
findings.matters: Lenders need clarity on the council's capital intensity, acceleration of delivery timelines, and the scale of funding required to support programme delivery. This affects sustainability of the funding strategy.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement rose from £762 million to £854 million; "it is a high year of spend as the Council has many projects on site in the HRA".
findings.quote: This was due to higher than planned levels of project delivery in key projects and consequent re-profiling of previously planned capital works. It is a high year of spend as the Council has many projects on site in the HRA (Godwin and Crowndale, Abbey Phase 3 and Camden and Chester Road hostels).

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account budget and rent review 2026 2027
findings.headline: Council freezes heating charges at 2025/26 levels while acknowledging risk of gas price rises from October 2026
findings.detail: The heating pool deficit has been repaid, allowing the council to freeze heating scales at 2025/26 levels. However, the council acknowledges high uncertainty in gas pricing due to geopolitical tensions and supply disruptions, with risk of price rises from October 2026. If prices rise, the heating pool could return to deficit.
findings.matters: Shows the HRA's exposure to commodity price risk in a volatile market. An unplanned heating pool deficit would require emergency charges or reserve drawdown, compounding financial pressure at a time when reserves are already stretched.
findings.figures: Risk of price rises from October 2026 onwards due to supply chain disruption and geopolitical factors
findings.quote: The future pricing of gas is highly uncertain due to volatile international markets, geopolitical tensions, and climate-related factors. There is a risk of prices rising from October 2026, driven by supply chain disruptions, increased seasonal demand, and evolving global energy policies. By holding the heating scales flat, this is taking on risk if the prices rise that the heating pool could end up once again in deficit.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account budget and rent review 2026 2027
findings.headline: Insourcing of domestic gas boiler services from March 2026 adds new recurring revenue cost
findings.detail: Cabinet approved insourcing of domestic gas servicing to improve quality, replacing the BTU contract that ends March 2026. The budget includes one-off costs and ongoing staffing costs for the new insourced team, adding a discretionary expenditure commitment to HRA revenue.
findings.matters: Shows the council taking on operational and employment risk while HRA is under financial pressure. Quality improvements are desirable but the timing and cost commitment compounds existing budget strain.
findings.figures: Insourcing cost includes 'some one-off costs as well as the cost of the new insourced team' (not quantified)
findings.quote: The insourcing of domestic gas was approved by Cabinet in February 2025. This investment is designed to improve the quality of service and replaces the existing gas servicing contract with BTU which ends in March 2026. This budget includes some one-off costs as well as the cost of the new insourced team.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account budget and rent review 2026 2027
findings.headline: HRA reserves are at low levels relative to financial risk environment
findings.detail: While reserves meet formal policy, they are considered insufficient given the heightened risk environment. The council acknowledges reserves need bolstering over the medium term to build financial resilience in the face of volatile costs, regulatory burden, and income constraints.
findings.matters: Low reserves relative to risk environment means limited buffer for cost shocks, interest rate changes, or policy shifts. Affects the council's ability to borrow for investment and indicates financial fragility.
findings.figures: Reserve levels meet policy but are 'low in the context of heightened risk environment'
findings.quote: While our reserve levels comply with our reserves policy, they are considered low in the context of our heightened risk environment and so, do require bolstering over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account budget and rent review 2026 2027
findings.headline: Significant unmet investment needs across stock despite £709m invested since 2013
findings.detail: Even after the Better Homes programme delivered £709m in investment since 2013 (averaging £59m/year), the 2023 stock condition survey identified a 'huge investment gap'. Fire safety assessments are ongoing, new Building Safety Act requirements are emerging, and substantial unmet needs remain in communal heating, energy efficiency, and mechanical/electrical systems.
findings.matters: Shows the scale of deferred maintenance and regulatory compliance work exceeds the capital investment the HRA can afford. Indicates future service quality pressure and potential accelerated stock deterioration if investment gap is not closed.
findings.figures: £709m invested since 2013; £265m commissioned projects; £295m planned over next 5 years; unmet needs not quantified
findings.quote: However, there are significant unmet needs across the housing stock even with these budgets in place. In particular, there will be continued investment need in relation to fire safety as our assessments continue and the new requirements that have arisen from the Fire Safety Act (2021) and the Building Safety Act 2022, alongside the need for significant investment in communal heating beyond the budgets currently set aside.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account budget and rent review 2026 2027
findings.headline: Disrepair cases rising with no downward trend, adding legal and work costs
findings.detail: The council notes that disrepair cases have risen and are not falling year-on-year. Both the cost of carrying out disrepair works and legal/disbursement fees have increased. Budget allocation has historically been misaligned with actual need, and the council now acknowledges the need to fund this growing pressure.
findings.matters: Rising disrepair cases indicate worsening stock condition and tenant satisfaction issues. Unplanned growth in this category suggests either stock is ageing faster than anticipated or maintenance has been inadequate, with both carrying reputational and legal risk.
findings.figures: Disrepair cases described as rising and not falling year-on-year; costs described as historically high but budgets not aligned
findings.quote: Disrepair cases have risen which is causing pressure through the cost of carrying out the disrepair works and the increase cost in legal and disbursement fees. Historically these costs have been high, but the budgets have not been aligned, disrepair cases are not falling year on year and therefore we need to fund this pressure.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account budget and rent review 2026 2027
findings.headline: £235m fire and building safety capital costs must be funded from HRA rents, not government grants
findings.detail: £328m total capital is needed for fire and building safety work 2018-2028. The council received only £92m in government grants for Chalcots, Cromer and Birkenhead Street estates. The remaining £235m capital expenditure plus £4.9m annual revenue cost must come entirely from the HRA—directly from tenant rents and charges. No external funding has been made available for the majority of this regulatory compliance work.
findings.matters: Shows a massive unfunded regulatory burden falling entirely on tenants. This diverts rental income from routine maintenance, investment and new building, and indicates the council is absorbing a cost that would normally be government-funded, weakening the HRA's financial position.
findings.figures: £328m total required; £92m grants received; £235m capital + £4.9m annual revenue from HRA alone
findings.quote: the Council has only received £92m in government grant for the fire safety works on the Chalcots, Cromer and Birkenhead Street Estates but the remaining £235m capital expenditure and an annual revenue budget of £4.9m has had to be funded entirely from the HRA's own resources – rent and service charges paid by tenants and leaseholders. To date, no external government funding support has been made available.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account budget and rent review 2026 2027
findings.headline: £5m reserve drawdown planned for 2026/27 to balance budget
findings.detail: The council proposes a one-off drawdown from HRA reserves of up to £5m for 2026/27 if rent convergence is not approved. This amount may be reduced if convergence is implemented, but signals the HRA cannot balance on current income.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion erodes the HRA's financial buffer and ability to absorb shocks. Repeated annual drawdowns would rapidly deplete reserves and weaken financial resilience, affecting the council's borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Up to £5m drawdown for 2026/27; reduction only if rent convergence approved
findings.quote: it is recommended that there is a planned drawdown from reserves of up to £5m for 2026/27 to balance the budget. This amount may reduce if rent convergence is implemented from April 2026.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account budget and rent review 2026 2027
findings.headline: £16.4m projected HRA funding gap by 2030/31 without rent convergence policy
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy forecasts a widening gap between HRA expenditure and income. Even with rent convergence at £1/week, the gap falls only to £10.6m; at £2/week it reaches £4.8m. This signals the HRA cannot be self-sustaining without new policy or spending cuts.
findings.matters: Indicates ongoing structural insolvency without external support. A lender would see this as unsustainable and requiring either policy intervention or service reduction, affecting the council's ability to maintain its stock and meet obligations.
findings.figures: £16.4m gap 2030/31 (no convergence); £10.6m (£1/week convergence); £4.8m (£2/week convergence)
findings.quote: the resulting forecast is £16.4m gap between expenditure and income by the financial year 2030/31 if there is no Rent Convergence. If Rent Convergence is agreed at £1 per week, this gap decreases to £10.6m by 2030/31, and if agreed at £2 per week, the gap decreases to £4.8m by 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account budget and rent review 2026 2027
findings.headline: £201m cumulative rental income lost since 2016 due to government policy changes
findings.detail: Government decisions including the bedroom tax, rent cap policy shifts from RPI to CPI, removal of rent convergence, increased Right to Buy discounts, enforced rent reductions (2016-2020), and caps on increases have systematically reduced the HRA's rental income. This structural erosion means income has failed to keep pace with investment needs.
findings.matters: Shows the HRA's funding problem is not due to council mismanagement but government policy—affecting the ability to invest in stock and service borrowing. A lender needs to understand this is a policy-driven issue, not performance-based.
findings.figures: £201m cumulative loss since 2016; £33m lower income in 2025/26 than if policy had remained at CPI + 1%
findings.quote: As a result of previous government policy, it has been calculated that the HRA has lost £201m of rental income since 2016 and rental income is £33m lower in 2025/26 compared with what it would have received if the policy had been kept consistent at CPI + 1%

findings.paper_title: 13 Review of the Council’s Medium Term Financial Strategy Final
findings.headline: Current Medium Term Financial Strategy being extended by one year to 2026/27, with new deficit opening up over medium term despite current balance
findings.detail: The Council's current MTFS was agreed in January 2023 and was planned to run to end 2025/26. Cabinet is now being asked to extend it by one year to 2026/27. This extension is being made 'in recognition of significant changes to the Council's operating environment'. The paper states 'a new deficit is opening up over the medium term' driven by demographic pressures, inflation, interest rates, COVID-19 impacts, and cost-of-living crisis. The Council anticipates having to find 'further budget savings' to protect financial resilience, acknowledging that 'given the depth of savings which the Council has had to make since 2010, this will unquestionably be difficult'.
findings.matters: A one-year MTFS extension signals the Council cannot develop a credible multi-year plan. Combined with an opening medium-term deficit and admissions that finding further savings will be 'unquestionably difficult', this indicates the Council is entering a period of constrained planning and limited scope for new investment.
findings.figures: MTFS extended one year to 2026/27; significant savings already made since 2010; new medium-term deficit emerging
findings.quote: In recognition of these significant changes to the Council's operating environment, the Council will therefore extend its current Medium Term Financial Strategy by one year to 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 13 Review of the Council’s Medium Term Financial Strategy Final
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account overspend of £7.3m in 2025/26, driven by damp, mould, fire safety, and disrepair costs
findings.detail: The HRA is forecasting a £7.3m overspend for 2025/26, mainly driven by additional repair and maintenance costs including damp and mould, fire safety works, and legal costs relating to disrepair claims. Awaab's Law came into force 27 October 2025, giving social landlords fixed timelines to address emergency and damp and mould hazards, which will create additional cost pressures in 2026/27. The Council has committed to insourcing gas servicing and additional revenue contributions to capital for housing asset management.
findings.matters: HRA overspends signal failure to maintain social housing to legal and safety standards, creating liability for disrepair claims. For a lender, this indicates capital underinvestment and regulatory risk.
findings.figures: £7.3m forecast HRA overspend 2025/26; £3.2m actual HRA overspend 2024/25
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account is forecasting to overspend by £7.3m this year. This is mainly driven by additional repair and maintenance costs across the social housing stock, with additional costs for damp and mould, fire safety and other repair costs.

findings.paper_title: 13 Review of the Council’s Medium Term Financial Strategy Final
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review expected to redirect funding away from Inner London boroughs, creating medium-term deficit risk
findings.detail: The government's Fair Funding Review 2.0 (announced June 2025) proposes substantial changes to how central government funding is distributed to councils through a new three-year settlement from 2026/27. Camden provided consultation responses in September 2025, and the government issued updated proposals in November 2025. The indications are that the review is expected to lead to 'some level of funding redirected away from Inner London boroughs such as Camden to other areas deemed to have high needs'. Final funding allocations are expected in December 2025. The Council is extending its current MTFS by one year to 2026/27 specifically to respond to these changes and the uncertainty they create.
findings.matters: A funding reduction on top of existing demand pressures would force the Council into deeper savings or deficit. The one-year MTFS extension signals the Council expects to need to find significant new savings but cannot yet plan what they will be.
findings.figures: Three-year settlement expected 2026/27-2028/29; final allocations expected December 2025; MTFS extended by one year to 2026/27
findings.quote: These changes are expected to see some level of funding redirected away from Inner London boroughs such as Camden to other areas deemed to have high needs without the local resources to meet them.

findings.paper_title: 13 Review of the Council’s Medium Term Financial Strategy Final
findings.headline: General reserves being drawn down to cover overspends, weakening financial resilience and ability to invest
findings.detail: The Council made a significant drawdown from reserves in 2024/25 to cover the £22.8m General Fund overspend. The Council will need to call on reserves again to cover 2025/26's forecast £19m overspend. Unearmarked general balances stood at £18.36m (5.9% of net budgeted expenditure) at the start of 2025/26, down from higher levels pre-pandemic. The Council budgets for £1.5m annual contributions to unearmarked general reserves, but continued overspends mean these cannot be replenished. The CIPFA Resilience Index notes Camden as relatively higher risk on the rate at which reserves are being used.
findings.matters: Reserves are the Council's financial shock absorber. When they fall below prudent levels, the Council loses flexibility to manage service pressures, invest in prevention, or respond to emergencies. A lender would flag reserve depletion as a precursor to liquidity stress.
findings.figures: £18.36m unearmarked general balances (5.9% of net expenditure) start 2025/26; £1.5m budgeted annual contribution; significant drawdown 2024/25; forecast further drawdown 2025/26
findings.quote: When money is drawn down from reserves and not replenished in equal or greater proportion, reserves start to deplete, increasing the risk to the Council's financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: 13 Review of the Council’s Medium Term Financial Strategy Final
findings.headline: Schools in deficit rose to 12 in 2024/25, up from 8, with 41% of schools drawing on reserves
findings.detail: School reserves were reduced by £5.8m in 2024/25 as schools managed budget pressures from wage increases, rising energy costs, and falling pupil rolls. The number of schools operating in deficit increased to 12 (from 8 previously), and 41% of all schools had to draw on reserves to support operational costs (up from 32% in 2023/24). Camden has experienced a 25% real-terms reduction in DSG Schools Block funding since 2011 due to falling pupil numbers (2,250 pupils lost between 2019 and 2024, resulting in £4.5m annual reduction).
findings.matters: Widening school deficits signal systemic funding failure across the education system. Once school reserves deplete, deficits cannot be written off; they become claims on the Council's General Fund or trigger intervention from the Department for Education.
findings.figures: 12 schools in deficit (up from 8); 41% of schools drawing on reserves (up from 32%); £5.8m reserve reduction; 25% real-terms funding cut since 2011; 2,250 pupils lost 2019-24; £4.5m annual funding reduction
findings.quote: The number of schools operating in deficit rose to 12, up from 8 the previous year, indicating a widening financial vulnerability.

findings.paper_title: 13 Review of the Council’s Medium Term Financial Strategy Final
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block reserve forecast to go into deficit in 2025/26, risking total DSG reserve deficit from 2026/27
findings.detail: Camden's High Needs Block reserve was £5.4m at the start of 2025/26, following a £4.9m drawdown in 2024/25. The forecast drawdown for 2025/26 is £8.1m, which would push the HNB reserve into deficit. This would require funding the shortfall from other DSG balances, leaving a forecast total DSG reserve of only £10.8m by end of 2025/26. The total DSG reserve could go into deficit from 2026/27 onwards if rising demand for EHCPs continues without additional government funding. The government has extended statutory override protections until March 2028.
findings.matters: DSG reserve depletion is a leading indicator of service cost failure. The Council cannot write off school deficits; once DSG reserves deplete, pressures transfer directly to the General Fund or force revenue service cuts.
findings.figures: £5.4m HNB reserve start 2025/26; £8.1m forecast drawdown; £10.8m forecast total DSG reserve end 2025/26; £4.9m drawdown 2024/25
findings.quote: At the end of Quarter 2, the HNB is forecast to require a drawdown of £8.1m from the DSG reserves. This would cause the HNB reserve to go into deficit in 2025/26

findings.paper_title: 13 Review of the Council’s Medium Term Financial Strategy Final
findings.headline: Children's social care placements forecast £2.5m overspend in 2025/26; average residential cost £5,300/week, joint-funded placements £12,000-£21,000/week
findings.detail: Children's social care placements overspent by an unspecified amount in 2024/25 and are forecasting a £2.5m overspend in 2025/26. Costs have increased significantly over ten years, driven by more children entering care, higher complexity of needs, and decline in in-house foster carers. Average residential placement cost is approximately £5,300 per week, with some joint-funded placements at £12,000-£21,000 per week. A capital investment of £11.1m was agreed in March 2025 for acquisition of properties for children's homes, but there is a risk costs will persist rising into 2026/27.
findings.matters: Rising placement costs per child combined with rising numbers in care creates a structural, long-term cost pressure that cannot be resolved by temporary contingencies. The wide variation in placement costs (£5,300 to £21,000/week) suggests pricing discipline remains weak.
findings.figures: £2.5m forecast overspend 2025/26; £5,300 average weekly residential cost; £12,000-£21,000 for complex joint-funded placements; £11.1m capital investment agreed March 2025
findings.quote: the average weekly cost is approximately £5,300, due to rising costs and complex needs. There are also some high-cost joint funded placement costs ranging from £12,000 - £21,000 per week.

findings.paper_title: 13 Review of the Council’s Medium Term Financial Strategy Final
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation now forecasting £8.5m net overspend despite £12m contingency, on expenditure of £26.4m
findings.detail: The Council's forecast net expenditure on temporary accommodation for 2025/26 is £26.4m, representing a £20.5m overspend against service budgets. Even after setting aside £12m in contingency, a £8.5m net overspend remains. London Councils research from October 2025 estimates a £740m temporary accommodation shortfall across London. Backlog issues with rent accounts and Housing Benefit claims have required significant resources to address.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is now the single largest uncontrolled cost driver for the Council. A lender would see this as a service where supply and funding mechanisms have fundamentally broken down, with no clear path to resolution in the forecast period.
findings.figures: £26.4m forecast expenditure; £20.5m overspend; £8.5m net overspend after contingency; £740m London-wide shortfall
findings.quote: The Council's forecast net expenditure on temporary accommodation for 2025/26 was £26.4m as at the end of September 2025. This represents a £20.5m overspend against service budgets.

findings.paper_title: 13 Review of the Council’s Medium Term Financial Strategy Final
findings.headline: General Fund overspend of £19m forecast for 2025/26, following £22.8m actual overspend in 2024/25
findings.detail: Despite £12m contingency for temporary accommodation and £9m for children's placements in the 2025/26 budget, the Council is forecasting a £19m overspend at Quarter Two. The previous year's £22.8m overspend was unprecedented. Officers are working to reduce these figures through the year, but demand volatility in social care and homelessness creates a range of forecasts.
findings.matters: Consecutive large overspends force the Council to draw on finite reserves, directly weakening its financial resilience and capacity to invest. For a lender, this signals deteriorating budget control and unsustainable service cost trajectories.
findings.figures: £19m forecast General Fund overspend 2025/26; £22.8m actual 2024/25
findings.quote: In 2024/25, the Council saw an unprecedented overspend of £22.8m in its General Fund and £3.2m in its Housing Revenue Account (HRA).

findings.paper_title: 15 Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 and Pension Fund Completion Report
findings.headline: Pension Fund accounts contain an immaterial £0.843m valuation adjustment on investment fair values.
findings.detail: The audit identified a £0.843m valuation difference on the fair value of Pension Fund investments, which will be recorded as an unadjusted misstatement. This was the only material finding in the Pension Fund audit.
findings.matters: Pension fund valuation accuracy affects the council's overall balance sheet strength and pension liability disclosure.
findings.figures: £0.843m unadjusted misstatement on fair value of investments.
findings.quote: an immaterial valuation difference of £0.843m on fair value of investments, which will be recorded as an unadjusted misstatement.

findings.paper_title: 15 Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 and Pension Fund Completion Report
findings.headline: The Pension Fund audit will result in a qualified opinion for 2024/25 because rebuilding assurance on opening balances is taking more than one year.
findings.detail: Despite completing the full 2024/25 audit work, the council will not receive an unqualified opinion in 2024/25. The auditor is rebuilding assurance on opening balances from prior disclaimed opinions, a process expected to extend beyond one financial year.
findings.matters: Continued qualified opinions indicate structural audit issues and may affect the council's creditworthiness assessment.
findings.figures: Backstop date 27 February 2026; rebuilding assurance process spans more than one year.
findings.quote: The process of rebuilding assurance is expected to take more than one financial year, and as such the council will not receive an unqualified opinion in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: 15 Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 and Pension Fund Completion Report
findings.headline: An objection to the Council's draft Annual Governance Statement is currently under auditor review.
findings.detail: An external objection to the accounts has been received relating to the Council's Annual Governance Statement. The auditors are conducting an independent assessment, with results to be reported to the Committee.
findings.matters: External governance objections may signal material control weaknesses or transparency issues that a lender would need to understand.
findings.figures: None provided; outcome of assessment not yet known.

findings.paper_title: 15 Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 and Pension Fund Completion Report
findings.headline: Camden received disclaimed audit opinions on 2022/23 and 2023/24 Council accounts due to insufficient audit completion time.
findings.detail: In both 2022/23 and 2023/24, Camden's Council accounts were not fully audited by the backstop deadline, resulting in disclaimed opinions rather than audit opinions. This indicates the council has struggled to meet the MHCLG backstop audit deadlines introduced in September 2024.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can meet statutory financial reporting deadlines and whether audit control weaknesses exist.
findings.figures: Backstop deadline for 2024/25 is 27 February 2026.
findings.quote: Due to insufficient time to fully complete the 2022/23 audits by the backstop deadline, Camden received a disclaimed audit opinion on both its Council and Pension Fund accounts. For 2023/24 the auditor again issued a disclaimed opinion on the Council accounts due to insufficient time to complete the audit

news_drafts.headline: Camden repays £29m LOBO loan after lender proposed 7.77%, replacing it with PWLB borrowing at 4.69%
news_drafts.lead:
Camden Council repaid a £29m bank loan on 27 August 2026 after the lender, FMS Wertmanagement, proposed raising its interest rate from 4.625% to 7.77%. The loan was a LOBO loan (a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher rate and the council may then repay in full instead of accepting it). The council's Audit and Corporate Governance Committee, meeting on 24 September, received the details in a treasury management update (a report on how the council borrows and manages its cash).

FMS notified the council of the proposed rise on 20 August. The council used its right to repay rather than accept. On 2 September it took out a replacement £29m loan for two years from the PWLB (Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils) at 4.69%, a rate that includes a discount for its housing revenue account (the ring-fenced account for council homes). The paper puts the new loan's interest at about £1.360m a year, which it says avoids about £893,000 a year compared with the FMS rate. It costs about £19,000 a year more than the original loan did.

The paper lists three more FMS loans with lender option dates: £15m on 24 September, £25m on 9 October and £10m on 29 October, £50m in all. It says further borrowing or refinancing (replacing old loans with new ones) may be needed during 2026/27, depending on "lender decisions, cash flow requirements, capital financing obligations, and prevailing interest rates".
